cards.a: Toussaint Louverture led an enslaved people's revolution that overthrew French colonial rule and slavery in Saint-Domingue (Haiti) in the 1790s. It terrified southern slaveholders, shaped U.S. refusal to recognize Haiti, and later encouraged Napoleon to sell Louisiana.
cards.h: → leader + what it overthrew + U.S. reaction
cards.n: A direct link between the Haitian Revolution and the 1803 Louisiana Purchase's origin.

cards.q: Identify the Adams-Onis Treaty of 1819 and its terms.
cards.a: A treaty in which Spain ceded Florida to the United States and gave up its claim to the Pacific Northwest, in exchange for the U.S. dropping claims to Texas and assuming $5 million in American citizens' claims against Spain. It also fixed the western boundary of the Louisiana Purchase.
cards.h: → Spain gives up Florida + boundary line set
cards.n: Negotiated by Secretary of State John Quincy Adams; often paired with the Monroe Doctrine on the timeline.

cards.q: Identify the 'Corrupt Bargain' of 1824.
cards.a: When no candidate won an electoral majority in the four-way 1824 race, the House of Representatives chose John Quincy Adams over Andrew Jackson, who had won the most popular and electoral votes. Adams then named Henry Clay, who had also run, as secretary of state, and Jackson's furious supporters called it a corrupt bargain.
cards.h: → House picks Adams over Jackson + Clay's reward
cards.n: Fueled Jackson's 1828 campaign and the birth of the Democratic Party as a movement against elite manipulation.

cards.q: Explain why the election of 1828 is considered a turning point toward mass democracy.
cards.a: Nearly all states had dropped property requirements for white male voters, and turnout roughly tripled from 1824. Jackson's campaign used mass rallies, parades, and slogans to appeal directly to ordinary voters, a style of popular politics that defined the new Second Party System.
cards.h: → expanded suffrage + turnout surge + campaign style
cards.n: The gain in democracy was for white men only; it coincided with tightening restrictions on free Black voters in several states.

cards.q: Define the Tariff of Abominations of 1828.
cards.a: A high protective tariff on manufactured imports, passed to help northern industry, that Southerners condemned as favoring the North while raising the cost of goods and inviting British retaliation against southern cotton exports. It set off the nullification crisis.
cards.h: → high tariff + why South hated it

cards.q: Define Calhoun's theory of nullification as laid out in the South Carolina Exposition and Protest.
cards.a: John C. Calhoun's 1828 argument that because states had created the Union, a state convention could declare a federal law unconstitutional and void within its borders, and even secede if overruled. South Carolina applied this theory to nullify the 1828 and 1832 tariffs.
cards.h: → author + core claim + which law it targeted
cards.n: A states' rights argument later echoed, in modified form, by secessionists in 1860-61.

cards.q: Explain how Jackson's Indian removal policy defied the Supreme Court's ruling in Worcester v. Georgia.
cards.a: The Court ruled that Georgia's laws did not apply within Cherokee territory, which fell under federal authority alone. Jackson refused to enforce the decision, reportedly saying Marshall could enforce it himself, and pushed forward with removal, leading to the Trail of Tears.
cards.h: → Court sides with Cherokee → Jackson ignores it
cards.n: A stark example of executive defiance of judicial authority, with no constitutional remedy available.

cards.q: Identify the American Colonization Society.
cards.a: An organization founded in 1816 that promoted resettling free Black Americans to Africa, founding the colony of Liberia in 1822. Many white members saw it as a moderate alternative to abolition; most free Black Americans and later abolitionists rejected it as racist.
cards.h: → goal + colony founded + why it was rejected
cards.n: A useful contrast to Garrison's later immediatist abolitionism, which explicitly repudiated colonization.

cards.q: Identify Nat Turner's Rebellion and give its year.
cards.a: In 1831, enslaved preacher Nat Turner led an uprising in Southampton County, Virginia, that killed about 55 white people before being suppressed. Turner and dozens of enslaved people, many uninvolved, were executed in the aftermath.

cards.q: Explain how Nat Turner's Rebellion changed the South's approach to slavery.
cards.a: Southern states passed much stricter slave codes banning Black literacy and independent Black churches, and southern legislatures largely abandoned public debate over gradual emancipation. It pushed proslavery writers toward defending slavery as a 'positive good' rather than a necessary evil.
cards.h: → stricter codes + end of emancipation debate
cards.n: The Virginia legislature had actually debated gradual emancipation in early 1832, its last such debate before the Civil War.

cards.q: Identify the Panic of 1819 and its main cause.
cards.a: The first major peacetime financial crisis in U.S. history, triggered when the Bank of the United States tightened credit after a land and cotton speculation boom collapsed. It caused widespread bank failures, unemployment, and debtor anger that fed both Missouri crisis tensions and Jacksonian politics.
cards.h: → first major panic + tight credit → collapse
cards.n: Deepened distrust of the national bank that Jackson later drew on in the Bank War.

cards.q: Identify Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott.
cards.a: Two abolitionist women who, after being barred from full participation at an 1840 world anti-slavery convention because of their sex, organized the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention and co-wrote the Declaration of Sentiments.
cards.h: → barred from abolition convention → organized Seneca Falls

cards.q: Identify Sojourner Truth.
cards.a: A formerly enslaved woman who became a powerful abolitionist and women's rights speaker, famous for challenging assumptions about race and gender in public addresses such as her 'Ain't I a Woman' speech.
cards.h: → formerly enslaved + dual cause + famous speech
cards.n: Her career links the abolition and women's rights movements, which drew heavily on shared activists.

cards.q: Identify the congressional gag rule of 1836-1844.
cards.a: A House rule automatically tabling all antislavery petitions without discussion, adopted to silence the flood of abolitionist petitions. Former president John Quincy Adams, then a congressman, led the fight to repeal it as a violation of the right to petition.
cards.h: → tables petitions + Adams leads repeal fight

cards.q: Contrast the 'necessary evil' and 'positive good' defenses of slavery.
cards.a: Earlier southern leaders such as Jefferson called slavery a necessary evil, an unfortunate inherited system to be phased out eventually. After the 1830s, writers like Calhoun instead argued slavery was a positive good that civilized and cared for an inferior race better than northern wage labor did.
cards.h: → regrettable system vs. actively beneficial system
cards.n: The shift reflects Nat Turner's Rebellion, abolitionist pressure, and the booming cotton economy after the cotton gin.

cards.q: Identify the Free Soil Party and its founding year.
cards.a: A third party founded in 1848 that opposed the expansion of slavery into western territories, uniting antislavery Whigs, Democrats, and Liberty Party members under the slogan 'free soil, free labor, free men.' It nominated former president Martin Van Buren in 1848.
cards.n: Distinguish from abolitionists: most Free Soilers opposed slavery's spread for economic and racial reasons, not out of concern for enslaved people.

cards.q: Identify the Ostend Manifesto of 1854.
cards.a: A secret memo by U.S. diplomats in Europe proposing that the United States buy Cuba from Spain, or take it by force if Spain refused, in order to add another slave state. Its leak caused a northern uproar over an apparent slaveholder conspiracy to expand slave territory.
cards.h: → proposal to acquire Cuba + why it caused outrage
cards.n: Fits the pattern of aggressive slave-power expansionism alongside Kansas-Nebraska in the same year.

cards.q: Identify the Confiscation Acts of 1861-1862.
cards.a: Union laws authorizing the seizure of Confederate property, including enslaved people used to support the rebellion, and declaring escaped slaves who reached Union lines free. They moved the war's aims toward emancipation before the Emancipation Proclamation.
cards.h: → seize rebel property + freed enslaved people who reached Union lines
cards.n: An important legal stepping-stone that shows emancipation policy evolving gradually, not overnight.

cards.q: Identify the Union border states and explain why Lincoln handled them carefully.
cards.a: Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri, and Delaware were slave states that stayed in the Union. Lincoln avoided early emancipation moves partly to keep these states, especially Maryland (which surrounded Washington, D.C.) and Kentucky, from seceding and joining the Confederacy.
cards.h: → four slave states in the Union + why caution mattered
cards.n: Lincoln reportedly said he hoped to have God on his side but must have Kentucky.

cards.q: Identify the Copperheads.
cards.a: Northern Democrats, also called Peace Democrats, who opposed the Civil War and called for a negotiated peace with the Confederacy. Some faced arrest under Lincoln's suspension of habeas corpus for allegedly disloyal speech and organizing.
cards.n: Links to the wartime civil liberties debate: their most famous target, Clement Vallandigham, was arrested and exiled.

cards.q: Identify the Gettysburg Address and how it redefined the war's purpose.
cards.a: Lincoln's brief 1863 speech dedicating the Gettysburg battlefield cemetery reframed the Civil War as a struggle to preserve a nation dedicated to human equality, not merely to restore the Union, invoking the Declaration of Independence's 'all men are created equal.'
cards.h: → 1863 + reframes war around equality, not just Union

cards.q: Identify the Radical Republicans and their Reconstruction goals.
cards.a: Congressional Republicans, led by figures like Thaddeus Stevens and Charles Sumner, who wanted harsher terms for the defeated South, real protection for freedpeople's civil and voting rights, and in some cases land redistribution. They clashed repeatedly with Andrew Johnson's lenient approach.

cards.q: Identify Special Field Order No. 15 and its reversal.
cards.a: General William T. Sherman's January 1865 order set aside coastal land in Georgia and South Carolina for freed Black families in forty-acre plots, the origin of '40 acres and a mule.' President Andrew Johnson revoked the order later that year, returning the land to former Confederate owners.
cards.n: Its reversal is central evidence for arguments that Reconstruction failed to deliver economic independence to freedpeople.

cards.q: Identify the Ku Klux Klan Act (Enforcement Act) of 1871.
cards.a: A federal law giving the president power to use the army and suspend habeas corpus to suppress Klan violence against Black voters and Republican officials in the South. Grant used it to crush the Klan in South Carolina in 1871.
cards.h: → federal power to suppress Klan + used in SC

cards.q: Define the Redeemers and their political goal.
cards.a: White southern Democrats who organized to 'redeem' state governments from Republican and biracial rule during and after Reconstruction, using fraud, violence, and appeals to white supremacy to regain political control across the South by 1877.

cards.q: Explain why the Crittenden Compromise of 1860-61 failed to prevent secession.
cards.a: Senator John Crittenden proposed extending the Missouri Compromise line to the Pacific and permanently protecting slavery where it existed. Lincoln and Republicans rejected any extension of slavery into new territory, and the plan died in Congress just before the war began.
cards.n: The last serious compromise attempt; its failure shows how little room for compromise remained by 1861.

cards.q: Identify Hiram Revels and Blanche K. Bruce.
cards.a: Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first Black U.S. senator in 1870, and Blanche K. Bruce, also of Mississippi, became the second in 1875, both serving during Reconstruction before white Redeemer governments closed off Black political power.
cards.h: → first and second Black U.S. senators + state

cards.q: Explain how the 1866 Memphis and New Orleans riots affected Congressional Reconstruction.
cards.a: White mobs, often including police, killed dozens of Black residents in Memphis and New Orleans in 1866. Northern outrage over the violence helped Radical Republicans win the 1866 midterms and pass the more aggressive Reconstruction Acts of 1867.
cards.h: → mob violence → Radical Republican midterm win → Reconstruction Acts
cards.n: Direct causal link between southern violence and the shift toward Congressional (Radical) Reconstruction.

cards.q: Date Juneteenth and explain what it commemorates.
cards.a: June 19, 1865, the day Union troops reached Galveston, Texas, and announced enslaved people there were free, more than two years after the Emancipation Proclamation. It is now a federal holiday marking the end of slavery in the United States.

cards.q: Identify In re Debs (1895) and its significance for organized labor.
cards.a: The Supreme Court unanimously upheld a federal injunction that had jailed Pullman Strike leader Eugene V. Debs for defying a court order to stop the strike, ruling the government could use injunctions to protect interstate commerce and the mail from strikes.
cards.h: → upholds injunction against Debs + basis: interstate commerce
cards.n: Gave employers and courts a powerful anti-strike tool used against labor for decades before the Norris-LaGuardia Act (1932).

cards.q: Identify the Exodusters.
cards.a: Tens of thousands of Black southerners who migrated to Kansas in 1879, seeking farmland and escape from Redeemer-era violence and sharecropping debt, in one of the first major organized Black migrations after Reconstruction's end.
cards.n: A precursor, on a smaller scale, to the much larger Great Migration of the twentieth century.

cards.q: Define 'waving the bloody shirt' as a Gilded Age political tactic.
cards.a: The practice, mostly by Republican candidates, of reminding northern voters that the Democratic Party was the party of secession and rebellion, blaming Democrats for Civil War deaths to win votes long after the war ended.
cards.h: → Republicans invoke Civil War loyalty against Democrats
cards.n: Explains why national elections stayed close and issue-thin for much of the Gilded Age.

cards.q: Identify the closing of the open range in the mid-1880s.
cards.a: Cheap barbed wire, invented by Joseph Glidden in 1874, let farmers fence off the open grasslands that cattle drives had depended on, while brutal winters in 1886-87 killed huge numbers of cattle, ending the era of the long cattle drive and open-range ranching.
cards.h: → barbed wire + harsh winters → end of cattle drives

cards.q: Identify the National American Woman Suffrage Association (NAWSA) and its founding year.
cards.a: Founded in 1890 by the merger of two rival suffrage groups, NAWSA became the main national organization pursuing women's voting rights through state-by-state campaigns, later achieving the 19th Amendment in 1920 under Carrie Chapman Catt's leadership.

cards.q: Identify Coxey's Army.
cards.a: A march of several hundred unemployed workers led by businessman Jacob Coxey from Ohio to Washington, D.C., in 1894 to demand a federal public works program to create jobs during the depression that followed the Panic of 1893. Coxey was arrested for walking on the Capitol lawn.
cards.n: An early example of a mass march on Washington demanding federal economic action, a tactic later reused throughout the twentieth century.

cards.q: Identify the Panic of 1893.
cards.a: A severe economic depression triggered by railroad overbuilding and bank failures that produced roughly 20 percent unemployment, deepened the free silver debate, and helped fuel the Populist Party's surge before the 1896 election.

cards.q: Define the 'Solid South.'
cards.a: The near-total, one-party Democratic control of southern politics from Redemption through most of the twentieth century, secured through disfranchisement of Black voters and made possible by white southerners' shared hostility to Reconstruction-era Republican rule.
cards.h: → one-party Democratic control + how it was secured

cards.q: Contrast Coxey's Army with the Pullman Strike as responses to the depression of the 1890s.
cards.a: Coxey's Army was a peaceful, symbolic march petitioning the federal government for public works jobs. The Pullman Strike was a disruptive national rail boycott that turned violent and was crushed by federal troops and a court injunction under In re Debs.
cards.n: Both failed in the short term but showed workers demanding a federal, not just local, response to hard times.

cards.q: Explain why the Populist Party's 1896 fusion with the Democrats ultimately destroyed the party.
cards.a: Populists endorsed Democrat William Jennings Bryan rather than running their own candidate, hoping free silver alone could win. When Bryan lost, the Populist Party had already merged its identity and voters into the Democratic Party and could not survive as an independent force.
cards.n: A cautionary case study in third-party 'fusion' strategy for any essay on third parties in American politics.

cards.q: Identify the Ocala Demands of 1890.
cards.a: A Farmers' Alliance platform calling for free coinage of silver, a graduated income tax, direct election of senators, and government-run subtreasuries to provide farmers low-interest crop loans. It was the direct template for the Populist Party's 1892 Omaha Platform.

cards.q: Identify the American Protective Association.
cards.a: A nativist organization founded in 1887 that opposed Catholic immigration, spread anti-Catholic conspiracy theories, and lobbied for immigration restriction, reflecting Gilded Age hostility toward the 'new immigrants' arriving from southern and eastern Europe.
cards.n: The Gilded Age counterpart to the antebellum Know-Nothings.

cards.q: Identify the Statue of Liberty and Emma Lazarus's 'The New Colossus.'
cards.a: The Statue of Liberty, dedicated in New York Harbor in 1886, became a symbol of welcome to immigrants after Emma Lazarus's 1883 poem 'The New Colossus,' with its line 'give me your tired, your poor,' was engraved on its pedestal in 1903.

cards.q: Identify Helen Hunt Jackson's A Century of Dishonor and its influence.
cards.a: An 1881 book documenting the U.S. government's broken treaties and mistreatment of Native peoples. It stirred reform-minded sympathy that fed into the assimilationist push behind the 1887 Dawes Severalty Act, even though that act itself caused further harm.
cards.h: → 1881 book + fed reform push → Dawes Act
cards.n: An example of a well-intentioned reform critique producing a policy (allotment) that did lasting damage.

cards.q: Explain how the sinking of the USS Maine helped push the U.S. into the Spanish-American War.
cards.a: A U.S. battleship exploded and sank in Havana harbor in February 1898, killing over 260 sailors. Yellow press outlets blamed Spanish sabotage without proof, and 'Remember the Maine' became the rallying cry that pushed Congress toward war.
cards.h: → ship explodes + press blames Spain + slogan → war fever
cards.n: The explosion's actual cause (likely an internal coal-bunker fire) remains disputed; the point for APUSH is how the press used it.

cards.q: Explain why the United States annexed Hawaii in 1898.
cards.a: American sugar planters had already overthrown Hawaii's monarchy, Queen Liliuokalani, in 1893 with the help of U.S. Marines. Congress annexed the islands in 1898 to secure a coaling and naval station supporting American power in the Pacific during the Spanish-American War.

cards.q: Identify the holding of Lochner v. New York (1905).
cards.a: The Supreme Court struck down a New York law limiting bakers' work hours, ruling it violated employers' and workers' 'freedom of contract' protected by the 14th Amendment's due process clause. It became the symbol of the Court blocking Progressive economic regulation.
cards.h: → strikes down hours law + freedom of contract
cards.n: The 'Lochner era' (roughly 1905-37) describes decades of the Court using this reasoning against labor and welfare laws.

cards.q: Contrast the holdings of Lochner v. New York (1905) and Muller v. Oregon (1908).
cards.a: Lochner struck down a law limiting men's bakery hours as violating freedom of contract. Muller upheld a law limiting women's work hours, reasoning that women's health and childbearing role justified special protection, revealing the Court's gendered double standard on labor regulation.
cards.h: → men's hours struck down vs. women's hours upheld
cards.n: Muller's protective reasoning was later criticized by feminists for reinforcing women's unequal legal status.

cards.q: Identify the founding of the NAACP and give its year.
cards.a: The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People was founded in 1909 by a coalition including W.E.B. Du Bois and white progressive reformers, in response to ongoing lynching and the 1908 Springfield race riot, to pursue Black civil rights through legal action and lobbying.
cards.n: Its legal strategy eventually produced Brown v. Board of Education decades later.

cards.q: Identify the Niagara Movement.
cards.a: A civil rights organization founded by W.E.B. Du Bois and William Monroe Trotter in 1905 that demanded full political, civil, and social rights for Black Americans, rejecting Booker T. Washington's accommodationist approach. It was a direct forerunner of the NAACP.

cards.q: Identify the sinking of the Lusitania and give its year.
cards.a: A German U-boat sank the British passenger liner Lusitania in 1915, killing nearly 1,200 people including 128 Americans. It turned American public opinion against Germany, though the U.S. did not enter the war for two more years.
cards.n: Germany's pledge to limit submarine warfare after this sinking broke down by 1917, directly triggering U.S. entry.

cards.q: Identify the Selective Service Act of 1917.
cards.a: A law requiring young American men to register for the military draft, ultimately registering over 24 million men and inducting nearly 3 million into the armed forces for World War I, after volunteer enlistment proved far too slow.

cards.q: Identify Henry Ford and his contribution to 1920s mass production.
cards.a: Automaker Henry Ford perfected the moving assembly line for the Model T, drastically cutting production costs and prices. His 1914 'five-dollar day' wage also let his own workers afford the cars they built, fueling the era's consumer culture.
cards.h: → assembly line + Model T + five-dollar day

cards.q: Define welfare capitalism as practiced by 1920s employers.
cards.a: A strategy in which large companies offered workers benefits such as paid vacations, pensions, stock options, and recreational facilities, in order to build loyalty and discourage unionization without raising wages or accepting collective bargaining.
cards.n: It weakened union membership through the 1920s, right before the Depression exposed its limits.

cards.q: Identify the Bonus Army of 1932.
cards.a: Thousands of unemployed World War I veterans marched on Washington, D.C., in 1932 demanding early payment of a bonus promised for 1945. Army troops under General Douglas MacArthur forcibly dispersed their camp on Hoover's orders, badly damaging Hoover's already weak public image.
cards.h: → WWI vets demand bonus + violent dispersal → Hoover's image ruined

cards.q: Explain why the election of 1932 marked a political realignment.
cards.a: Franklin Roosevelt's landslide victory over Hoover built a durable New Deal Coalition of urban workers, immigrants, Catholics, Jews, Black voters outside the South, and white southerners, uniting behind an activist federal government that would dominate American politics for decades.
cards.h: → FDR wins big → New Deal Coalition forms
cards.n: This coalition, not the specific 1932 platform (which was still fairly cautious), is the lasting significance.

cards.q: Identify the Good Neighbor Policy.
cards.a: Franklin Roosevelt's 1933 policy formally renouncing U.S. military intervention in Latin America, replacing the Roosevelt Corollary's interventionism with diplomatic and economic engagement, including withdrawing Marines from Haiti and Nicaragua.
cards.n: A direct reversal of the Roosevelt Corollary (1904); a useful contrast pair across Period 7.

cards.q: Explain why Congress passed the Neutrality Acts of the 1930s.
cards.a: Disillusionment with U.S. entry into World War I, documented by the Nye Committee's claims that arms manufacturers had pushed the country into war for profit, drove Congress starting in 1935 to ban arms sales and loans to nations at war, in hopes of avoiding another European conflict.
cards.h: → WWI disillusionment + Nye Committee → ban arms sales
cards.n: FDR gradually chipped away at these laws (cash-and-carry, then Lend-Lease) as the Axis threat grew.

cards.q: Identify Rosie the Riveter and women's World War II workforce mobilization.
cards.a: A cultural icon representing the roughly six million American women who took factory and defense-industry jobs during World War II, filling labor shortages as men went to fight, alongside women who served in uniform through the WACs and WAVES.
cards.h: → icon + wartime factory work + military auxiliaries
cards.n: Most women left or were pushed out of these jobs after the war, though the experience shaped later feminist demands.

cards.q: Identify the Yalta Conference and give its year.
cards.a: A February 1945 meeting of Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin near the end of World War II that planned Germany's occupation into zones, Soviet entry against Japan, and free elections in liberated Eastern Europe, promises the Soviets soon broke.
cards.h: → 1945 + Big Three + broken promises on Eastern Europe
cards.n: Its broken promises are a standard opening cause cited for the Cold War.

cards.q: Identify the Nuremberg Trials.
cards.a: A series of military tribunals held in Nuremberg, Germany, from 1945 to 1946 that prosecuted top Nazi leaders for war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide, establishing the precedent that following orders was not a valid legal defense.

cards.q: Identify Executive Order 9981 and give its year.
cards.a: President Truman's 1948 order declaring equal treatment and opportunity in the U.S. armed forces regardless of race, which led to the desegregation of military units over the following several years, ahead of most civilian institutions.
cards.n: An early Cold War civil rights move: Truman worried segregation embarrassed the U.S. in its propaganda contest with the Soviets.

cards.q: Identify the Little Rock Nine and the 1957 crisis at Central High School.
cards.a: Nine Black students who integrated Little Rock Central High School in Arkansas in 1957 despite Governor Orval Faubus using the National Guard to block them. President Eisenhower federalized the Guard and sent Army troops to enforce the integration order.
cards.h: → 9 students + governor blocks + Eisenhower sends troops
cards.n: Shows the federal government's willingness, if reluctantly, to enforce Brown with military force.

cards.q: Identify the Eisenhower Doctrine and give its year.
cards.a: A 1957 policy pledging U.S. military and economic aid to any Middle Eastern nation resisting communist aggression or subversion, extending containment into a region destabilized by the Suez Crisis and declining British and French influence.

cards.q: Identify the U-2 incident of 1960.
cards.a: The Soviet Union shot down an American U-2 spy plane over its territory and captured pilot Francis Gary Powers. Eisenhower's initial denial was embarrassed by Soviet proof, and the incident wrecked a planned Paris summit and worsened Cold War tensions.
cards.h: → spy plane shot down + failed cover story

cards.q: Explain why East Germany built the Berlin Wall in 1961.
cards.a: Hundreds of thousands of East Germans were fleeing to the West through Berlin's open border each year, draining the East German economy of skilled workers. East Germany, backed by the Soviet Union, built a concrete wall in 1961 to seal the border and stop the exodus.
cards.h: → mass exodus west → wall seals the border
cards.n: It became the Cold War's most visible physical symbol of a divided Europe.

cards.q: Identify the Peace Corps.
cards.a: A federal volunteer program created by President Kennedy in 1961 that sent young Americans abroad to work on education, agriculture, and health projects in developing nations, combining humanitarian goals with a soft-power effort to counter Soviet influence.

cards.q: Identify the Taft-Hartley Act of 1947.
cards.a: A law passed over Truman's veto that curbed union power gained under the Wagner Act, banning the closed shop, allowing states to pass 'right-to-work' laws, and letting the president order an 80-day cooling-off period to delay strikes threatening national health or safety.
cards.n: Labor called it the 'slave labor act'; it marked the start of organized labor's postwar decline.

cards.q: Identify Truman's Fair Deal.
cards.a: Truman's postwar domestic program proposing an extension of New Deal liberalism, including national health insurance, an increased minimum wage, and civil rights legislation. A conservative coalition in Congress blocked most of its ambitious elements.
cards.h: → New Deal extension + what passed vs. blocked

cards.q: Explain why Congress passed the National Defense Education Act in 1958.
cards.a: The Soviet Union's 1957 Sputnik launch convinced American leaders the U.S. was falling behind in science and technology. The 1958 act funneled federal funding into science, math, and foreign language education and student loans to close the perceived gap.
cards.h: → Sputnik shock → federal funding for STEM education

cards.q: Identify the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965.
cards.a: A Great Society law providing the first major federal funding for K-12 public education, targeted especially at schools serving low-income students, greatly expanding the federal government's role in a policy area traditionally left to states and localities.

cards.q: Identify the Clean Air Act of 1970.
cards.a: A federal law, strengthened during the environmental movement's peak, that set national air quality standards and required states to reduce industrial and vehicle pollution, enforced by the newly created Environmental Protection Agency.
cards.h: → 1970 + national air standards + enforced by EPA

cards.q: Identify the holding of United States v. Nixon (1974).
cards.a: The Supreme Court unanimously ruled that executive privilege was not absolute and ordered President Nixon to turn over White House tape recordings sought in the Watergate investigation, a decision that led directly to his resignation.
cards.h: → rejects absolute executive privilege → tapes released
cards.n: A landmark check on executive power, decided unanimously even by Nixon's own appointees.

cards.q: Explain why Nixon's 1972 visit to China mattered for Cold War diplomacy.
cards.a: By opening relations with Communist China after more than two decades of hostility, Nixon exploited the growing Sino-Soviet split to gain diplomatic leverage over the Soviet Union, a striking example of detente-era pragmatism from a longtime anticommunist.
cards.h: → opens China relations + exploits Sino-Soviet split → leverage over USSR
cards.n: A striking reversal from the anticommunist Nixon of the 1950s Red Scare era.

cards.q: Identify Title IX and give its year.
cards.a: A 1972 federal law banning sex discrimination in any education program receiving federal funding, which dramatically expanded women's and girls' access to school athletics and professional and graduate programs over the following decades.
cards.h: → 1972 + bans sex discrimination in education + athletics impact

cards.q: Contrast the legislative fate of Truman's Fair Deal with Lyndon Johnson's Great Society.
cards.a: A conservative coalition of Republicans and southern Democrats blocked most of the Fair Deal in a closely divided Congress. Johnson, with huge Democratic majorities after 1964 and the political momentum from JFK's assassination, pushed most of the Great Society into law.
cards.h: → mostly blocked vs. mostly enacted + why (majorities)

cards.q: Explain why Eisenhower relied on covert CIA operations as a Cold War tool.
cards.a: Covert action, such as CIA-backed coups that overthrew elected governments in Iran (1953) and Guatemala (1954), let the U.S. remove leaders viewed as pro-Soviet without the cost, casualties, or diplomatic fallout of open military intervention.
cards.n: Both coups had long-term backlash: Iran's 1979 revolution and decades of anti-U.S. sentiment in Latin America.

cards.q: Date Executive Order 9981, Brown v. Board of Education, and the Little Rock crisis in order.
cards.a: Executive Order 9981 desegregated the armed forces in 1948, Brown v. Board of Education struck down school segregation in 1954, and the Little Rock Nine integrated Central High School amid federal troop enforcement in 1957.

cards.q: Identify the PATCO strike of 1981.
cards.a: When the Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization struck illegally for better pay and conditions, President Reagan fired over 11,000 striking controllers and banned them from federal service for life, signaling a new era of hostility toward organized labor.
cards.n: Often cited as the symbolic start of organized labor's steep decline in the 1980s.

cards.q: Explain why the election of 1980 is considered a realigning election.
cards.a: Ronald Reagan's decisive win over Jimmy Carter, amid stagflation and the Iran hostage crisis, brought together economic conservatives, evangelical Christians, and 'Reagan Democrats' disillusioned with liberalism into a durable New Right coalition that reshaped American politics for decades.
cards.h: → Reagan wins + coalition forms + why (economic/cultural discontent)

cards.q: Identify the World Trade Organization and give its founding year.
cards.a: An international body created in 1995 to replace the older GATT system, setting rules for global trade and resolving disputes between member nations. Its founding reflected and accelerated the rapid economic globalization of the 1990s.
cards.n: Critics on both left and right blamed it for job losses to overseas competition, fueling later anti-globalization protests.

cards.q: Explain why the United States invaded Afghanistan in October 2001.
cards.a: The Taliban government ruling Afghanistan refused to hand over al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden after the September 11 attacks. The U.S. invaded to topple the Taliban and destroy al-Qaeda's base of operations, opening what became America's longest war.
cards.h: → Taliban shelters al-Qaeda → invasion → longest war

cards.q: Identify the Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993.
cards.a: A federal law, one of Bill Clinton's first major signed bills, guaranteeing eligible employees up to twelve weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for childbirth, adoption, or family medical emergencies.
cards.h: → 1993 + unpaid job-protected leave + first Clinton bill

cards.q: Identify the 'Don't Ask, Don't Tell' policy and give its year.
cards.a: A 1993 Clinton administration compromise policy that let gay and lesbian Americans serve in the military only if they concealed their sexual orientation, banning the military from asking about it but also barring service members from disclosing it. It was repealed in 2011.

cards.q: Identify the Defense of Marriage Act and give its year.
cards.a: A 1996 federal law defining marriage as between one man and one woman for federal purposes and letting states refuse to recognize same-sex marriages performed elsewhere. The Supreme Court struck down its federal-recognition provision in United States v. Windsor (2013).

cards.q: Explain the rise and collapse of the dot-com bubble.
cards.a: Investors poured money into internet startups in the late 1990s on hopes of explosive future growth, driving stock prices far above the companies' actual earnings. When many of these unprofitable firms failed in 2000-2001, the bubble burst, wiping out trillions in market value.

cards.q: Identify Citizens United v. FEC (2010) and its holding.
cards.a: The Supreme Court ruled that restricting independent political spending by corporations and unions violated the First Amendment's free speech protections, opening the door to unlimited outside spending in elections through super PACs.
cards.n: A frequently cited turning point in debates over money's role in modern American politics.

cards.q: Identify the Tea Party movement.
cards.a: A grassroots conservative movement that emerged in 2009 opposing federal bailouts, the Affordable Care Act, and government spending, pushing the Republican Party rightward on fiscal and constitutional issues and helping fuel major Republican gains in the 2010 midterms.

cards.q: Contrast the Tea Party and Occupy Wall Street movements.
cards.a: The Tea Party, emerging in 2009, blamed government spending and bailouts and pushed politics rightward through electoral organizing. Occupy Wall Street, emerging in 2011, blamed corporate greed and economic inequality, organizing through decentralized protest camps rather than electoral politics.
cards.n: Both arose from the same 2008 financial crisis but diagnosed the cause, and proposed opposite solutions, to it.

cards.q: Identify Obergefell v. Hodges and give its year.
cards.a: A 2015 Supreme Court decision holding that the 14th Amendment guarantees same-sex couples the right to marry, legalizing same-sex marriage nationwide and overturning remaining state bans.

cards.q: Identify the Black Lives Matter movement.
cards.a: A decentralized civil rights movement that emerged in 2013 after the acquittal of George Zimmerman in the shooting of Trayvon Martin, growing into nationwide protests against police violence and racial injustice, especially after the 2014 killing of Michael Brown in Ferguson, Missouri.
cards.n: Often framed as a continuation of the long civil rights movement using social media organizing tools unavailable in the 1960s.

cards.q: Date the founding of the WTO, NAFTA's implementation, and the 2008 financial crisis in order.
cards.a: NAFTA took effect in January 1994, the World Trade Organization was founded in 1995, and the global financial crisis struck in 2008, tracing the arc from accelerating globalization to its most severe modern economic shock.

cards.q: Identify the Great Law of Peace and the two legendary founders credited with uniting the Iroquois nations.
cards.a: The Gayanashagowa, an oral constitution establishing the Iroquois Confederacy's council of clan-chosen chiefs. Tradition credits the Huron prophet Deganawida and the Onondaga orator Hiawatha with persuading the five founding nations to end blood feuds and unite.
cards.n: Some scholars argue the Confederacy's consensus-based council influenced Enlightenment ideas about federalism, though the claim is debated.

cards.q: Define the two-spirit gender role recognized in many pre-contact Native societies.
cards.a: A person, usually assigned male or female at birth, who took on a distinct social and spiritual role blending or crossing conventional gender lines, often serving as healers, mediators, or ceremonial leaders. The role existed among diverse peoples including the Zuni, Lakota, and Navajo.
cards.n: Colonial and later U.S. missionaries actively suppressed this role; its documentation comes mostly from oral tradition and later ethnography.

cards.q: Identify La Malinche (Malintzin) and her role in the Spanish conquest of Mexico.
cards.a: A Nahua woman given to Cortes in 1519 who became his interpreter, adviser, and later mother of his son. Her linguistic skill helped Cortes negotiate alliances with Aztec rival city-states, making her indispensable to the conquest and a lasting, contested symbol in Mexican memory.
cards.n: Later nationalist memory recast her as a traitor (malinchismo), a reading many historians now push back against.

cards.q: Identify the Taino people and their experience as the first Native population to meet Spanish colonizers.
cards.a: An Arawak-speaking people who inhabited the Caribbean islands, including Hispaniola, when Columbus arrived in 1492. Forced labor under the encomienda system, combined with famine and Old World disease, destroyed most of the Taino population within a generation.
cards.n: Taino cultural and genetic legacy persisted through intermarriage in the Caribbean far more than the 'extinction' narrative once assumed.

cards.q: Identify the Kingdom of Kongo's conversion to Christianity under King Afonso I and its connection to the early slave trade.
cards.a: Afonso I converted to Catholicism and built diplomatic ties with Portugal in the early 1500s, but Portuguese demand for captives drew Kongo into supplying the Atlantic slave trade even as its king protested the trade's abuses to the Portuguese crown.
cards.n: A useful case against treating Africa as simply passive: Kongo's rulers negotiated with, not just fell victim to, Europeans.

cards.q: State the historiographical debate over how many people lived in the Americas before 1492.
cards.a: Older estimates put the pre-contact population near 1 million north of Mexico; researchers like Henry Dobyns argued for tens of millions across the hemisphere. The range matters because higher estimates make post-contact demographic collapse far more catastrophic.
cards.n: A frequently tested historiography point: the estimate you choose changes how devastating you judge the Columbian Exchange to have been.

cards.q: Define the Black Legend (Leyenda Negra).
cards.a: A depiction of Spanish colonization as uniquely cruel and fanatical, spread partly through Bartolome de las Casas's writings and amplified by Spain's Protestant rivals, England and the Netherlands, for propaganda purposes.
cards.n: Historians now note English and French colonization involved comparable violence; the Legend served rival empires' self-image.

cards.q: Contrast the Spanish economic model of mining and tribute with the French economic model of the fur trade in early colonization.
cards.a: Spain extracted silver and gold through forced Native and African labor under encomienda and mining drafts, building permanent settlements and mission towns. France relied on small trading posts and alliances with Native hunters to acquire furs, requiring cooperation rather than conquest.
cards.n: Fewer French settlers meant less land displacement of Native peoples in the interior, compared to Spanish and later English patterns.

cards.q: Define the tribute system that funded the Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan.
cards.a: Conquered city-states across central Mexico paid the Aztec Triple Alliance regular tribute in goods, food, and captives for sacrifice, collected by officials called calpixque. The burden bred deep resentment that Cortes later exploited to recruit Native allies.

cards.q: Identify Giovanni da Verrazzano's and Jacques Cartier's voyages and what they established for France.
cards.a: Verrazzano explored the North American coast for France in 1524; Cartier explored the St. Lawrence River in 1534-1535. Together their voyages gave France its claim to the region that became New France.
cards.n: France's thin settlement pattern, trading posts rather than farms, later shaped its more cooperative relations with Native nations.

cards.q: Define the 'seasoning' period newly arrived enslaved Africans endured on Caribbean sugar plantations.
cards.a: A brutal one-to-three-year adjustment period in which new captives were forced to acclimate to plantation labor, disease environments, and harsh discipline. Mortality during seasoning was extremely high, especially in the sugar islands.
cards.n: Seasoning mortality rates as high as one-third help explain the sugar islands' constant demand for new captives.

cards.q: Explain how Hispaniola's early sugar-and-slave economy became the template later exported to Barbados and Carolina.
cards.a: Spanish planters on Hispaniola combined African slave labor with sugar cultivation as early as the 1510s. English planters later copied this sugar-slavery model in Barbados, which colonists then carried directly to South Carolina.

cards.q: Identify Tisquantum (Squanto) and his role in the Plymouth colony's survival.
cards.a: A Patuxet man who had learned English after being kidnapped by an English sea captain years earlier. He taught the Plymouth Pilgrims to plant corn and fish, and served as interpreter with the Wampanoag sachem Massasoit in 1621.
cards.n: The 1621 harvest feast popularly called the 'First Thanksgiving' was a diplomatic event, not the origin of the national holiday, which dates to Lincoln's 1863 proclamation.

cards.q: Define feme covert and its effect on colonial women's legal status.
cards.a: The common-law doctrine that a married woman's legal identity merged into her husband's, so she could not own property, sign contracts, or sue in her own name. An unmarried woman, a feme sole, retained those legal rights.

cards.q: Explain why most people accused of witchcraft at Salem in 1692 were women.
cards.a: Most accused were women, especially those who were widowed, unmarried, or held property outside male control, since they defied expectations of female subordination. Economic anxiety and family land disputes in Salem Village sharpened suspicion of such women.
cards.h: → women outside male control + land disputes
cards.n: Historian Carol Karlsen's research on Salem found accused women disproportionately stood to inherit property, undercutting purely religious explanations.

cards.q: Explain the push and pull factors that drew German and Scots-Irish migrants to the colonial backcountry in the early eighteenth century.
cards.a: Push factors included land scarcity, high rents, and religious persecution in the German Palatinate and Ulster. Pull factors included cheap Pennsylvania land, religious toleration, and reports from earlier migrants, drawing both groups down the Great Wagon Road into the backcountry.
cards.n: The Scots-Irish backcountry migration also intensified conflict with Native peoples already settled in the Appalachian foothills.

cards.q: Define the putting-out system of colonial household production.
cards.a: A system in which merchants supplied raw materials, such as wool or flax, to rural families who spun and wove them into cloth at home for a set fee, allowing manufacturing to happen outside any central workshop.
cards.n: The putting-out system persisted alongside factories well into the nineteenth century in trades like shoemaking.

cards.q: Identify Henry Hudson's 1609 voyage and the claim it gave the Dutch.
cards.a: Hudson, sailing for the Dutch East India Company, explored the river that bears his name in 1609, giving the Netherlands its claim to the region that became New Netherland.

cards.q: Identify the Covenant Chain linking the Iroquois Confederacy to the English colonies.
cards.a: A series of alliances beginning in the 1670s between the Iroquois Confederacy and English colonial governments, especially New York, coordinating trade and diplomacy and giving the Iroquois leverage as brokers between the English and other Native nations.
cards.n: Iroquois diplomatic leverage from the Covenant Chain declined sharply after their losses in the Revolution.

cards.q: Identify the Tuscarora War of 1711-1715 and its long-term result for the Iroquois Confederacy.
cards.a: A war between North Carolina settlers and the Tuscarora people that ended in Tuscarora defeat. Many survivors migrated north and were adopted into the Iroquois Confederacy around 1722, making it the Six Nations.

cards.q: Explain the economic importance of naval stores production in colonial North Carolina.
cards.a: Colonists tapped the region's pine forests for tar, pitch, and turpentine used to waterproof and maintain British naval ships. Parliament paid bounties for naval stores to reduce dependence on Baltic imports, tying North Carolina's economy to the Royal Navy's needs.

cards.q: Explain the economic role colonial women played as 'deputy husbands' managing farms and businesses.
cards.a: Wives routinely ran farms, shops, and even ships' business affairs when husbands traveled or died, despite lacking independent legal standing. This practical authority, though temporary and derivative of a husband's, gave many women real economic experience.
cards.h: → practical authority despite no legal standing

cards.q: Identify the Massachusetts School Law of 1647 (the 'Old Deluder Satan' Act).
cards.a: A law requiring Massachusetts towns of 50 or more families to hire a schoolteacher and towns of 100 or more to establish a grammar school, so children could read the Bible and resist Satan's deception through ignorance.
cards.n: This law is the direct ancestor of the American tradition of public, tax-funded education.

cards.q: Identify Eliza Lucas Pinckney and her development of indigo as a South Carolina cash crop.
cards.a: A young planter who, managing her father's South Carolina estates in the 1740s, experimented with West Indian indigo seed until she produced a marketable dye crop. Indigo became the colony's second staple alongside rice.

cards.q: Date Jonathan Edwards's Northampton revival and George Whitefield's colonial preaching tour in sequence.
cards.a: Edwards's Northampton, Massachusetts revival began in 1734-1735; Whitefield's colony-wide preaching tour, which turned local revivals into a shared intercolonial movement, ran from 1739 to 1741.
cards.h: → Edwards local first, then Whitefield intercolonial

cards.q: Identify the role of the Dutch West India Company in bringing the first documented Africans to English Virginia.
cards.a: A Dutch trading company active in the Atlantic slave trade whose ship brought the first documented Africans to Virginia in 1619, selling about twenty captives at Jamestown.
cards.n: Their exact legal status in 1619, servant or slave, remains debated; Virginia's slave codes did not formalize hereditary racial slavery until decades later.

cards.q: Contrast Hamilton's and Jefferson's visions of the ideal American economy.
cards.a: Hamilton favored a diversified economy of manufacturing, finance, and cities, funded by a national bank and tariffs, with wealthy creditors tied to the government's success. Jefferson favored a republic of independent farmers, distrusted banks and cities, and saw agriculture as the guarantor of civic virtue.
cards.n: This economic-vision contrast underlies nearly every First Party System fight, from the Bank to the Whiskey Rebellion to the Louisiana Purchase.

cards.q: Identify Hamilton's Report on Manufactures (1791) and its central argument.
cards.a: A report to Congress proposing federal tariffs and subsidies to encourage domestic manufacturing and reduce dependence on British imports. Congress rejected its subsidy proposals but later used protective tariffs to pursue similar goals.

cards.q: Identify the Compromise of 1790 (the 'dinner table bargain').
cards.a: An agreement, reportedly brokered over dinner by Jefferson, Madison, and Hamilton, in which southern representatives accepted federal assumption of state war debts in exchange for locating the new national capital on the Potomac River.
cards.n: Some historians doubt the dinner really settled the deal single-handedly, since both issues had separate momentum already.

cards.q: Define the compact theory of the Union laid out in the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions.
cards.a: The argument, written by Jefferson and Madison in 1798, that the Constitution was a compact among sovereign states, so a state could judge federal laws unconstitutional and refuse to enforce them, as Kentucky and Virginia proposed to do with the Alien and Sedition Acts.
cards.n: This is the direct ancestor of Calhoun's nullification theory in Period 4.

cards.q: State what the Naturalization Act of 1798 changed and why the Federalists wanted it.
cards.a: It extended the residency requirement for U.S. citizenship from five to fourteen years. Federalists, who saw recent immigrants as likely Democratic-Republican voters, hoped the longer wait would slow their path to the ballot box.

cards.q: Explain how the Iroquois Confederacy split during the American Revolution.
cards.a: The Confederacy's tradition of unanimous consent broke down as the Oneida and Tuscarora sided with the Patriots while the Mohawk, Seneca, Cayuga, and Onondaga sided with the British. The resulting civil war shattered two centuries of Confederacy unity.
cards.h: → Oneida/Tuscarora Patriot vs other four British

cards.q: Identify Abigail Adams's 'Remember the Ladies' letter to John Adams.
cards.a: A March 1776 letter urging her husband and the Continental Congress to grant women legal protection against arbitrary treatment by husbands as they designed a new government, warning that women would 'foment a rebellion' if ignored.
cards.n: John Adams's dismissive reply shows how marginal even sympathetic Founders considered women's legal claims at the time.

cards.q: Identify Judith Sargent Murray and her argument in 'On the Equality of the Sexes.'
cards.a: An essayist who argued in 1790 that women's apparent intellectual inferiority resulted from unequal education, not innate ability, and called for expanded female schooling, an early Enlightenment-era feminist argument.

cards.q: Explain why Virginia and other states without large war debts opposed Hamilton's assumption plan.
cards.a: States like Virginia had already paid off much of their Revolutionary War debt, so assuming other states' debts meant their taxpayers would help cover obligations they had already settled, a transfer they viewed as unfair.

cards.q: State what the Coinage Act of 1792 established.
cards.a: It created the U.S. Mint in Philadelphia and established a bimetallic dollar based on both gold and silver, giving the new nation its own standardized currency for the first time.

cards.q: Identify St. Clair's Defeat of 1791 and the Native leaders who won it.
cards.a: The Western Confederacy, led by Miami chief Little Turtle and Shawnee chief Blue Jacket, destroyed General Arthur St. Clair's army in the Ohio Country, the worst defeat the U.S. Army ever suffered against Native forces, before Fallen Timbers reversed the outcome in 1794.
cards.h: → Little Turtle + Blue Jacket, worst U.S. defeat

cards.q: Explain how the Revolutionary War expanded colonial women's economic responsibilities.
cards.a: With men away fighting, women managed farms, shops, and finances, made decisions about planting and trade, and sometimes ran family businesses for years. This wartime necessity gave many women unaccustomed economic authority, though it rarely translated into lasting legal rights.
cards.h: → wartime necessity, not lasting legal change

cards.q: Identify the 'Molly Pitcher' legend and the broader role of women who followed the Continental Army as camp followers.
cards.a: Molly Pitcher is a composite legend, often linked to Mary Ludwig Hays, symbolizing women who carried water and sometimes took up arms at battles like Monmouth. Thousands of women served armies as camp followers, cooking, nursing, and doing laundry.
cards.n: Most named 'camp follower' women were poor and enslaved, a fact the patriotic Molly Pitcher legend tends to obscure.

cards.q: Differentiate the funding of the national debt from the assumption of state debts in Hamilton's financial plan.
cards.a: Funding meant paying off federal Revolutionary War debt at full face value to establish government credit. Assumption meant the federal government additionally taking on the states' separate war debts, a distinct and more controversial step that shifted state obligations onto the nation.
cards.h: → federal debt paid vs state debts absorbed

cards.q: Identify Charles Grandison Finney and the 'burned-over district.'
cards.a: Finney was the leading revivalist preacher of the Second Great Awakening, known for emotional 'anxious bench' conversions. Upstate New York, swept so repeatedly by revivals that observers said no one was left unconverted, became known as the burned-over district.
cards.n: Finney's revivals drew heavily on women converts, who then carried reform energy into temperance and abolition societies.

cards.q: Identify John Humphrey Noyes and the Oneida Community's practice of 'complex marriage.'
cards.a: Noyes founded the Oneida Community in New York in 1848 on the belief that Christ's Second Coming had already occurred, freeing members from conventional sin. Complex marriage rejected monogamy, treating all adult members as married to one another under group oversight.
cards.n: Noyes fled to Canada in 1879 to avoid prosecution once outside pressure over complex marriage grew too strong.

cards.q: Identify Mother Ann Lee and the Shaker practice of celibacy.
cards.a: Lee founded the Shakers in America in the 1770s, teaching that celibacy and communal property ownership would perfect believers. Shaker communities practiced gender-equal leadership but relied on conversion and adoption, not birth, to survive.

cards.q: Identify George Ripley and Brook Farm.
cards.a: Ripley, a transcendentalist minister, founded Brook Farm in Massachusetts in 1841 as a cooperative community where manual and intellectual labor were shared equally. Nathaniel Hawthorne briefly lived there before satirizing the experiment in The Blithedale Romance.

cards.q: Identify the Hudson River School and explain what its landscape paintings expressed.
cards.a: A group of painters led by Thomas Cole who depicted the American wilderness on a grand, romanticized scale. Their work expressed nationalist pride in a landscape untouched by Europe's history and reflected transcendentalist reverence for nature.

cards.q: Identify Margaret Fuller and her contribution to transcendentalism and early feminist thought.
cards.a: Fuller edited the transcendentalist journal The Dial and wrote Woman in the Nineteenth Century (1845), arguing that women deserved the same access to self-development and intellectual independence that transcendentalism promised men.
cards.h: → The Dial editor + early feminist tract
cards.n: Fuller later became the first female foreign correspondent for a major U.S. newspaper, reporting on the 1848 Roman Republic.

cards.q: Define minstrelsy and its role in antebellum popular culture.
cards.a: A wildly popular stage entertainment in which white performers wore blackface makeup to mock and stereotype enslaved and free Black Americans. Figures like Thomas D. Rice, creator of 'Jump Jim Crow,' made minstrel shows the dominant form of American mass entertainment by the 1840s.
cards.n: Minstrelsy shaped white Americans' racial imagination well beyond the stage; the term 'Jim Crow' later named segregation laws.

cards.q: Contrast republican motherhood with the cult of domesticity.
cards.a: Republican motherhood, from the 1780s-90s, cast women's household role as civic: raising virtuous male citizens for the new republic. The cult of domesticity, emerging with the market revolution after 1830, cast the home as a private moral refuge from a competitive commercial world, disconnected from direct civic purpose.
cards.h: → civic child-rearing vs private moral refuge
cards.n: Both confined women to the home but justified it with different logic, one political, one economic.

cards.q: Date the sequence of transportation improvements in the market revolution: turnpikes, canals, and railroads.
cards.a: Private turnpikes spread from the 1790s through the 1820s; the Erie Canal, completed in 1825, triggered a canal-building boom through the 1830s; railroads then overtook canals as the dominant carrier from the 1830s through the 1850s.

cards.q: Differentiate the putting-out system from the Lowell factory system.
cards.a: The putting-out system paid rural families to spin and weave cloth at home on their own schedule. The Lowell system gathered young unmarried women into centralized mills with power looms, company boardinghouses, and fixed factory hours under close supervision.
cards.h: → home-based, own pace vs mill, fixed hours

cards.q: Identify Tecumseh and Tenskwatawa (the Shawnee Prophet) and their pan-Indian resistance movement.
cards.a: Tecumseh organized a confederacy of Native nations to resist U.S. expansion by refusing to recognize land cessions made by individual tribes, while his brother Tenskwatawa provided religious inspiration urging rejection of white culture and alcohol. William Henry Harrison broke the movement at Tippecanoe in 1811.
cards.n: Tecumseh's death fighting for the British at the Battle of the Thames (1813) effectively ended organized pan-Indian resistance east of the Mississippi.

cards.q: Identify the Treaty of New Echota (1835) and why it was considered fraudulent.
cards.a: A treaty ceding all Cherokee land east of the Mississippi in exchange for western land and payment, signed by a small unauthorized 'Treaty Party' faction rather than the elected Cherokee government under Chief John Ross. The Senate ratified it anyway, providing the legal basis for the Trail of Tears.
cards.n: John Ross petitioned Congress against the treaty with thousands of Cherokee signatures, but removal proceeded regardless.

cards.q: Identify the Maine Law of 1851.
cards.a: The first statewide prohibition law in the United States, banning the manufacture and sale of alcohol except for medicinal and industrial purposes. A dozen other states copied it within a few years before most repealed or weakened their versions by the Civil War.

cards.q: Identify Harriet Tubman and the Underground Railroad.
cards.a: An escaped enslaved woman who returned to the South roughly thirteen times to guide about seventy enslaved people to freedom via the Underground Railroad, a loose network of secret routes and safe houses. She later served the Union Army during the Civil War.
cards.h: → escaped conductor + network of safe houses

cards.q: Date the Panic of 1857 and explain why it deepened sectional tension.
cards.a: A financial crisis triggered in August 1857 by railroad overinvestment and falling grain prices hit northern banks, factories, and railroads hard, while cotton prices stayed strong, letting southerners argue slavery-based agriculture was economically superior and 'cotton is king.'

cards.q: Identify the Dakota War of 1862 in Minnesota.
cards.a: A conflict in which the Dakota Sioux, facing broken treaty payments and starvation, attacked settlers in Minnesota. After suppressing the uprising, the U.S. carried out the largest mass execution in American history, hanging 38 Dakota men in December 1862.
cards.n: Lincoln personally reviewed the 303 death sentences and commuted all but 38, still the largest mass execution ordered by a U.S. president.

cards.q: Identify the Sand Creek Massacre of 1864.
cards.a: Colorado militia under Colonel John Chivington attacked a peaceful, flag-flying Cheyenne and Arapaho camp at Sand Creek, killing roughly 150 people, mostly women and children, despite the camp's chief having negotiated for protection.
cards.n: A congressional investigation later condemned Chivington's actions, but he was never criminally prosecuted.

cards.q: Identify Clara Barton and the U.S. Sanitary Commission's role in the Civil War.
cards.a: Barton organized battlefield nursing and supply distribution for wounded soldiers, later founding the American Red Cross in 1881. The U.S. Sanitary Commission, a civilian relief agency staffed largely by women volunteers, coordinated medical supplies and sanitation for the Union Army.

cards.q: Explain how the Civil War expanded northern women's paid employment outside the home.
cards.a: With men away fighting, women took paid jobs as government clerks, factory and arsenal workers, and mill hands in unprecedented numbers, work that had been almost entirely closed to women before the war, though most lost these positions once men returned.

cards.q: Identify the National Banking Acts of 1863-1864 and their purpose.
cards.a: Laws creating a system of federally chartered national banks that issued a uniform national currency backed by government bonds, replacing a chaotic mix of state bank notes and helping finance the Union war effort.

cards.q: Identify the 54th Massachusetts Regiment and its significance for Black soldiers in the Civil War.
cards.a: One of the first Black regiments raised in the North, led by white colonel Robert Gould Shaw, it fought with acclaimed courage at Fort Wagner in 1863. Nearly 200,000 Black soldiers, most organized as United States Colored Troops, ultimately served the Union.
cards.n: Black soldiers initially received lower pay than white soldiers; the 54th refused all pay for over a year in protest until Congress equalized it in 1864.

cards.q: Identify the Long Walk of the Navajo.
cards.a: In 1864, the U.S. Army under Kit Carson forced roughly 8,000 Navajo people to march over 300 miles to internment at Bosque Redondo, New Mexico, where hundreds died of disease and starvation before the Navajo were allowed to return to a reservation in 1868.

cards.q: Identify Harriet Tubman's role as a Union Army scout during the Civil War.
cards.a: Tubman served as a nurse, spy, and armed scout for the Union, and in 1863 guided the Combahee Ferry Raid in South Carolina, which freed roughly 700 enslaved people, making her the first woman to lead a U.S. military operation.

cards.q: Explain why the woman suffrage movement split into two rival organizations in 1869.
cards.a: Stanton and Anthony formed the National Woman Suffrage Association to oppose the 15th Amendment for excluding women and to push for a federal suffrage amendment. Lucy Stone's American Woman Suffrage Association supported the 15th Amendment as it stood and favored a state-by-state strategy.

cards.q: Identify the Colfax Massacre of 1873 and the Supreme Court case that followed it.
cards.a: A white paramilitary force killed up to 150 Black militiamen defending the Colfax, Louisiana courthouse, the deadliest single act of Reconstruction violence. In United States v. Cruikshank (1876), the Court overturned the killers' convictions, ruling the 14th Amendment did not restrain private individuals.
cards.n: Cruikshank gutted the Enforcement Acts by holding that the 14th Amendment restrained only state action, leaving Klan violence by private citizens beyond federal reach.

cards.q: Identify the Civil Rights Act of 1866.
cards.a: The first federal civil rights law, passed over Andrew Johnson's veto, declared all persons born in the United States (except Native Americans) citizens with equal rights to make contracts, own property, and sue in court. Congress soon wrote its guarantees into the 14th Amendment to secure them from repeal.
cards.h: → first civil rights law + basis of 14th Amendment

cards.q: Identify Red Cloud's War and the Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868.
cards.a: Oglala Lakota chief Red Cloud led a successful campaign against U.S. forts protecting the Bozeman Trail. The resulting Fort Laramie Treaty forced the Army to abandon the forts and recognized the Black Hills as part of the Great Sioux Reservation, one of the few outright Native military victories in the Plains wars.
cards.n: The treaty's Black Hills guarantee collapsed after gold was found there in 1874, a good example of treaty rights ignored when resources were at stake.

cards.q: Define greenbacks and explain the constitutional fight over paper currency resolved in the Legal Tender Cases.
cards.a: Greenbacks were paper currency the Union issued starting in 1862 without gold or silver backing, valid legal tender by government decree. The Supreme Court initially struck down using them to pay pre-war debts in Hepburn v. Griswold (1870), then reversed itself the next year in the Legal Tender Cases.
cards.h: → paper money by decree + Court reversal

cards.q: Identify vaudeville as a form of Gilded Age mass entertainment.
cards.a: A variety stage show combining comedy, music, acrobatics, and novelty acts, performed in theater circuits across growing industrial cities. Vaudeville drew mixed working- and middle-class urban audiences and became the dominant popular entertainment before movies replaced it.
cards.h: → variety stage shows + urban mass audience

cards.q: Identify Coney Island as a symbol of Gilded Age commercialized leisure.
cards.a: A Brooklyn beachfront resort that grew into a massive amusement district by the 1890s, with roller coasters, sideshows, and dance halls drawing millions of working- and middle-class New Yorkers seeking affordable escape from crowded, industrial city life.

cards.q: Identify the founding of professional baseball's National League in 1876.
cards.a: The National League organized professional baseball into a stable business with standardized rules and franchises, turning the sport into the era's leading spectator pastime and a shared cultural touchstone across growing industrial cities.

cards.q: Identify the Woman's Christian Temperance Union and Frances Willard's 'Do Everything' policy.
cards.a: Founded in 1874, the WCTU was the largest women's organization of the era, campaigning against alcohol. Under Frances Willard it adopted a 'Do Everything' policy linking temperance to broader reforms, including woman suffrage, labor rights, and prison reform.
cards.n: The WCTU shows how a 'respectable' women's cause became a training ground for wider political organizing, including suffrage.

cards.q: Contrast the Greenback Party's currency demands with the postwar push to resume specie payments.
cards.a: The Greenback Party, active from 1874 into the 1880s, demanded keeping and expanding paper currency to inflate prices and ease farmers' debt burdens. Conservative 'hard money' advocates pushed the Resumption Act of 1875, which returned greenbacks to gold convertibility by 1879, favoring creditors over debtors.
cards.h: → more paper money vs return to gold

cards.q: Name the main nativist organizations in order from the 1850s through the 1920s: Know-Nothings, APA, Immigration Restriction League, and the second Klan.
cards.a: The Know-Nothings (American Party) targeted Irish and German Catholics in the 1850s; the American Protective Association targeted Catholics from 1887; the Immigration Restriction League pushed a literacy test from 1894; the revived Ku Klux Klan of the 1920s targeted Catholics, Jews, and immigrants nationwide.
cards.n: Notice the escalation: from party politics (Know-Nothings) to lobbying (APA, IRL) to a mass paramilitary-adjacent fraternal order (1920s Klan).

cards.q: Identify the Immigration Restriction League and its proposed literacy test.
cards.a: Founded by Boston elites in 1894, the League lobbied for a federal literacy test to exclude illiterate immigrants, aiming disproportionately at the 'new immigrants' from southern and eastern Europe. Congress passed a literacy test in 1917 over Wilson's veto.

cards.q: Identify the Chautauqua movement.
cards.a: A traveling and later stationary adult education movement, founded in New York in 1874, that brought lectures, concerts, and religious instruction to small towns, giving the rural middle class access to culture and self-improvement outside formal schooling.
cards.h: → traveling adult education for rural towns

cards.q: Identify the Carlisle Indian Industrial School and Richard Henry Pratt's assimilationist motto.
cards.a: Founded in 1879 by Richard Henry Pratt, Carlisle was the model for federal boarding schools that removed Native children from their families to force assimilation, cutting their hair and banning Native languages under Pratt's motto to 'Kill the Indian, and save the man.'
cards.h: → Pratt's boarding school + forced assimilation motto

cards.q: Identify Susan B. Anthony's 1872 arrest for voting.
cards.a: Anthony voted illegally in the 1872 presidential election to test whether the 14th Amendment's citizenship guarantee implied a right to vote for women. She was arrested, tried, and fined, refusing to pay, but the courts rejected her constitutional argument.

cards.q: Identify Lillian Wald and the Henry Street Settlement.
cards.a: Wald founded the Henry Street Settlement on New York's Lower East Side in 1893, pioneering public health nursing for immigrant families and helping launch the visiting nurse movement alongside her settlement work.
cards.h: → Lower East Side + public health nursing

cards.q: Explain how the Dawes Act and boarding schools like Carlisle pursued the same assimilationist goal by different means.
cards.a: The Dawes Act broke up communally held reservation land into individual allotments to replace tribal identity with individual landowning citizens. Boarding schools pursued the same end culturally, stripping Native children of language, dress, and religion to remake them as assimilated Americans.
cards.h: → land allotment + cultural stripping, same goal

cards.q: Define the company town model of industrial paternalism practiced at Pullman, Illinois.
cards.a: George Pullman built a planned town where employees rented company-owned housing and bought from company stores, with rent deducted directly from wages. When wages fell in the 1894 depression but rents did not, workers' resentment fueled the Pullman Strike.

cards.q: Date the founding of the WCTU and the merger that created the National American Woman Suffrage Association.
cards.a: The Woman's Christian Temperance Union was founded in 1874. The rival National and American woman suffrage associations reunited in 1890 to form the National American Woman Suffrage Association (NAWSA).

cards.q: Identify Thomas Edison's electric light and Alexander Graham Bell's telephone as symbols of Gilded Age technological change.
cards.a: Bell patented the telephone in 1876 and Edison introduced a practical incandescent light bulb in 1879, both transforming daily communication and urban life and symbolizing the era's rapid pace of technological innovation.

cards.q: Identify Zora Neale Hurston's contribution to the Harlem Renaissance.
cards.a: Hurston combined anthropological fieldwork on southern Black folklore with fiction, most famously the novel Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), celebrating Black vernacular culture rather than presenting it for white approval.
cards.h: → folklore + Their Eyes Were Watching God

cards.q: Identify Duke Ellington's residency at the Cotton Club and its significance.
cards.a: Ellington led his orchestra at Harlem's Cotton Club from 1927 to 1931, broadcasting nationally over radio. The club excluded Black patrons even as it showcased Black performers, exposing white audiences nationwide to jazz while illustrating the era's persistent segregation.

cards.q: Identify Langston Hughes's essay 'The Negro Artist and the Racial Mountain.'
cards.a: A 1926 manifesto in which Hughes argued Black artists should express authentic Black experience without regard to whether it pleased white or Black middle-class audiences, resisting pressure toward respectability.

cards.q: Contrast the 1920s flapper with the Victorian ideal of womanhood she rejected.
cards.a: The Victorian ideal prized modesty, domesticity, and deference. The flapper cut her hair short, wore short skirts and makeup, smoked and drank in public, and pursued paid work and sexual freedom, symbolizing a new, more independent version of young womanhood.

cards.q: Explain why the Panic of 1907 led directly to the creation of the Federal Reserve System.
cards.a: When the 1907 panic hit, only J.P. Morgan's private intervention prevented a full banking collapse, exposing the danger of relying on one banker to manage a national crisis. Congress created the Federal Reserve in 1913 to give the government its own tool to stabilize banks and currency.
cards.h: → Morgan's private bailout exposed the gap
cards.n: The Fed's founders deliberately built a decentralized system of regional reserve banks, a compromise between fear of Wall Street control and fear of pure government control.

cards.q: State the specific quota formulas of the Emergency Quota Act of 1921 and the National Origins Act of 1924.
cards.a: The 1921 act capped immigration from each nation at 3 percent of that nationality's U.S. population as of the 1910 census. The 1924 act tightened this to 2 percent based on the 1890 census, a baseline chosen specifically to shrink quotas for southern and eastern Europeans.
cards.n: The 1890 baseline is the tested detail: choosing an earlier census before the 'new immigration' surge was a deliberate way to favor northern and western Europeans.

cards.q: Explain how New Deal deficit spending anticipated Keynesian economics before Keynesian theory was fully adopted.
cards.a: John Maynard Keynes argued government spending could revive demand during a depression, and New Deal relief and public works programs put this logic into practice even before Keynes's General Theory (1936) was widely accepted, though FDR's own deficits remained too small to end the Depression fully.
cards.n: Full-scale Keynesian deficit spending during World War II, not the New Deal itself, is what actually ended the Depression.

cards.q: Identify the Bretton Woods Conference of 1944 and the international monetary system it created.
cards.a: Forty-four Allied nations met in New Hampshire in 1944 to design a postwar monetary order pegging currencies to the U.S. dollar, itself convertible to gold, and creating the International Monetary Fund and World Bank to stabilize global trade and finance.

cards.q: Explain how the 'Brandeis Brief' shaped the Supreme Court's reasoning in Muller v. Oregon (1908).
cards.a: Louis Brandeis's brief relied mainly on sociological and medical data about the physical toll of long working hours on women, rather than legal precedent, persuading the Court to uphold Oregon's maximum-hours law for women as protecting maternal health.
cards.n: This 'sociological jurisprudence' approach became a model for later reform litigation, though it also cemented the sexist premise that women alone needed such protection.

cards.q: Explain what happened to Rosie the Riveter's wartime factory jobs after 1945.
cards.a: As veterans returned seeking work, employers laid off or reassigned millions of women from wartime industrial jobs, and postwar culture pushed a return to domesticity. Many working-class and Black women, who had worked out of necessity, quietly stayed in the paid workforce.
cards.h: → postwar layoffs + push back to domesticity
cards.n: Government propaganda that had urged women into factories in 1942 flipped almost overnight in 1945 to urge them back into the home.

cards.q: Identify the Zoot Suit Riots of 1943.
cards.a: White servicemen stationed in Los Angeles attacked Mexican American youths wearing zoot suits, seen as unpatriotic given wartime fabric rationing. The violence lasted several days before military authorities intervened, exposing wartime racial and ethnic tension.
cards.h: → LA 1943 + servicemen attack Mexican American youth

cards.q: State the effect of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 on the Great Depression.
